ferritin.origin: The Mayo female reference interval of 6 to 175 µg/L is a statistical range for apparently healthy adults; the catalogue cites textbook chapters only (Henry’s, 2007; Tietz, 2012 and 2018) and no reference-interval study [S1]. The Mayo text states that ferritin shows no sex difference before puberty and that female values rise with age [S1]. Labcorp reports 15 to 150 ng/mL for adult women but states that it “has adopted a threshold of 30 ng/mL in adult and adolescent patients, to identify patients with iron deficiency” [S2].
ferritin.sexSpecificWhat: WHO 2020 threshold for risk of iron overload in apparently healthy individuals (>150 µg/L in menstruating women; >200 µg/L in men and non-menstruating women). The WHO iron-deficiency threshold (<15 µg/L from 5 years of age) is identical for both sexes.
ferritin.contestedSummary: The WHO <15 µg/L threshold is expert opinion graded as low certainty; its evidence review found a mean ferritin of 15.1 µg/L (9 studies, 390 participants) where bone-marrow iron was absent [S4]. In 7,498 non-pregnant women aged 15 to 49 (NHANES), Mei et al. (2021) found that haemoglobin began to decline below a ferritin of 25.2 µg/L (95% CI 24.2 to 26.2) and soluble transferrin receptor to rise below 24.0 µg/L (23.3 to 24.6); at this threshold the US prevalence of iron deficiency in premenopausal women would rise from about 17% to about 30% [S5, S6]. The British Society of Gastroenterology (2021) states that values below 30 µg/L “are generally indicative of low body iron stores” and that a 45 µg/L threshold has specificity 0.92 [S7]; the American Society of Hematology (2026) raised its diagnostic threshold to 30 ng/mL irrespective of anaemia, with 50 ng/mL in higher-risk groups [S11, S12].
ferritin.guidanceInBand: The British Society of Gastroenterology (2021) states: “SF levels of less than 30 µg/L are generally indicative of low body iron stores”; “The cancer risk in iron deficiency without anaemia is low”; and “There is insufficient evidence to support invasive investigation in non-anaemic iron deficiency” [S7]. WHO (2020) states that, with infection or inflammation, “a ferritin concentration below 30 μg/L in children and 70 μg/L in adults may be used to indicate iron deficiency” [S4].
ferritin.labRangeSource: Mayo Clinic Laboratories, test FERR1 (female 18 to 50 years; ≥51 years: 11 to 328)

S12.title: ASH raises ferritin thresholds for diagnosing iron deficiency

haemoglobin.origin: For its complete blood count (CBC) intervals, Mayo cites Adeli et al. (2015), a CALIPER and Canadian Health Measures Survey study of 11,999 participants aged 3 to 79 measured on Beckman Coulter HmX and Sysmex analysers, which found that “females had lower hemoglobin and hematocrit starting at puberty” [H1, H3]. The WHO anaemia thresholds (120 g/L in women, 130 g/L in men) were first proposed in 1968 on the basis of “four published references and one set of unpublished observations” in European and North American populations; the WHO 2024 revision retained them, basing the adult values on fifth centiles of apparently healthy, iron-replete populations [H4].
haemoglobin.sexSpecificWhat: WHO 2024 haemoglobin threshold defining anaemia in non-pregnant women and men aged 15 to 65 (120 and 130 g/L); the CDC 1998 thresholds are 12.0 and 13.5 g/dL.
haemoglobin.contestedSummary: Beutler and Waalen (2006) excluded iron deficiency (transferrin saturation <16% or ferritin <10 µg/L) in 2,966 white women aged 20 to 49 and 6,709 white men aged 20 to 59 (Scripps-Kaiser), and a sex difference persisted: fifth centiles were 12.2 and 13.7 g/dL respectively [H5]. Braat et al. (2024), the WHO-commissioned pooled analysis, reported fifth centiles of 119.7 g/L (90% CI 119.1 to 120.3; n=3,640) in iron-replete non-pregnant women and 134.9 g/L (134.2 to 135.6; n=2,377) in men; WHO retained 120 g/L for women, and retained 130 g/L for men despite data “suggest[ing] a higher haemoglobin cutoff (i.e. 135 g/L)” [H4, H6]. Rushton et al. (2001) argued that the female reference limit had been derived from iron-deficient populations; the iron-replete data of Morison and Ferguson (ferritin 80 to 100 µg/L; 612 men, 1,327 women) showed 10th centiles of 139 and 123 g/L respectively and that a male reference range would misclassify 25 to 50% of women as anaemic [H10, H10a].
haemoglobin.guidanceInBand: WHO (2024) classifies 110 to 119 g/L in a non-pregnant woman as “Mild anaemia” and notes that management “could vary depending on the clinical scenario and the underlying cause(s)” [H4]. The British Society of Gastroenterology (2021) states: “iron deficiency should be confirmed by iron studies prior to investigation. Serum ferritin is the single most useful marker of IDA” [H9].
haemoglobin.labRangeSource: Mayo Clinic Laboratories, test CBC (≥18 years)

haematocrit.origin: As for haemoglobin, Mayo cites Adeli et al. (2015; Canadian Health Measures Survey, 11,999 participants aged 3 to 79) and the Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI) reference-interval standard EP28-A3c; Adeli et al. reported lower haematocrit in female participants from puberty [H1, H3]. The interval is a population centile, not an outcome-based threshold.
haematocrit.sexSpecificWhat: CDC 1998 haematocrit threshold for anaemia in non-pregnant women and men aged 18 years and over (5th percentile of NHANES III after exclusion of probable iron deficiency). The WHO 2024 guideline gives haemoglobin thresholds only.
haematocrit.contestedSummary: No haematocrit-specific threshold study was identified; the dispute derives from haemoglobin, for which iron-replete fifth centiles retain a sex difference (Beutler and Waalen, 2006; Braat et al., 2024) [H5, H6]. The range of disagreement is narrow: the Mayo female lower reference limit (35.5%) lies immediately below the CDC anaemia threshold (35.7%), so a value of 35.6% falls within the Mayo reference interval and below the CDC threshold [H1, H8].
haematocrit.guidanceInBand: CDC (1998) classifies a haematocrit below 35.7% in a non-pregnant woman as anaemia and states that a ferritin of 15 µg/L or less then “confirms iron deficiency in anemic women” [H8]. Mayo states: “Results should be interpreted in conjunction with the patient’s clinical picture and appropriate additional testing performed” [H1].
haematocrit.labRangeSource: Mayo Clinic Laboratories, test CBC (≥18 years)

transferrin_saturation.origin: The Mayo interval of 14 to 50% is supported by textbook and guideline citations only (Tietz, 7th ed., 2023; the American College of Gastroenterology (ACG) 2019 haemochromatosis guideline; Lopez et al., Lancet, 2016), with no reference-interval study cited; Mayo reports day-to-day intra-individual variation of “approximately 25% to 30%” and states that the test “should not be used as the primary test for iron deficiency” [T1]. The deficiency thresholds in use (16% and 20%) are conventions and not sex-partitioned centiles [T1, T4, T5].
transferrin_saturation.sexSpecificWhat: EASL 2022 transferrin saturation above which iron overload is suspected and HFE genotyping is recommended (with ferritin >200 µg/L in women and >300 µg/L in men). The iron-deficiency thresholds (<16%, CDC; <20%, BSG, and in the presence of inflammation) are identical for both sexes.
transferrin_saturation.contestedSummary: The Mayo reference interval begins at 14%, below both the CDC iron-deficiency threshold (<16%) and the <20% threshold of the British Society of Gastroenterology and of Mayo in inflammation; a value of 15 to 19% therefore falls within the laboratory reference interval while meeting a deficiency definition [T1, T4, T5]. The European Association for the Study of the Liver states “There is no universally accepted threshold for ferritin or transferrin saturation indicating iron overload” and adopts the sex-specific 45% and 50% values from a single population screening study [T3].
transferrin_saturation.guidanceInBand: Mayo states: “Percent saturation less than 16% is generally used to screen for iron deficiency, but a threshold of 20% is used in the presence of inflammation” [T1]. The British Society of Gastroenterology (2021) states: “A transferrin saturation of <20% is indicative of iron restriction” and “Transferrin saturation can help if a false-normal ferritin is suspected” [T5].
transferrin_saturation.labRangeSource: Mayo Clinic Laboratories, test SFEC (percent saturation; serum iron is sex-specific: male 50 to 150, female 35 to 145 mcg/dL)

mcv.origin: Mayo cites Adeli et al. (2015; Canadian Health Measures Survey, 11,999 participants aged 3 to 79, Beckman Coulter HmX or Sysmex analysers) and Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI) EP28-A3c; unlike haemoglobin and haematocrit, the adult MCV interval is not partitioned by sex [M1, M3]. Mayo defines microcytosis as MCV <80 fL [M1].
mcv.sexSpecificWhat: No sex-specific MCV threshold was identified in WHO, CDC or BSG documents; CDC defines low MCV as a value below the age-specific 5th percentile of NHANES III and reports no sex-specific values [M4].
mcv.contestedSummary: No published argument that the female MCV reference interval is derived from an inappropriate population was identified. The sole discrepancy is definitional: the Mayo lower reference limit (78.2 fL) differs from its microcytosis threshold (80 fL) [M1].
mcv.guidanceInBand: Mayo states: “Anemias are characterized as microcytic (MCV <80), macrocytic (MCV >100), or normocytic” and “iron deficiency anemia is characterized by a high RDW, while thalassemia is characterized by a low RDW” [M1]. The British Society of Gastroenterology (2021) states: “Age, sex, Hb concentration and mean cell volume are all independent predictors of risk of GI cancer in IDA” [M5].
mcv.labRangeSource: Mayo Clinic Laboratories, test CBC (≥18 years; identical for men and women)
